hook.text: A V8 cruising on a highway doesn't need all eight cylinders—half are doing nothing useful.

buildup.text: Running all cylinders at light load wastes fuel because each pumps air it can't fully use.

discovery.text: Cylinder deactivation shuts half the cylinders, closing their valves and cutting fuel delivery.

twist.text: The engine switches between four and eight cylinders so smoothly most drivers never notice.

climax.text: GM's Active Fuel Management saves up to 8 percent on highway fuel consumption.

punchline.text: Half the cylinders nap while the other half work harder.

quiz.question: What does cylinder deactivation do at light engine loads?
options: Shuts down some cylinders to save fuel

details.summary: Cylinder deactivation shuts down half of an engine's cylinders during light loads like highway cruising, reducing fuel consumption by eliminating pumping losses and friction in the deactivated cylinders.
details.whyItMatters: Big engines spend most of their time barely loaded. Cylinder deactivation lets a V8 run as an efficient four-cylinder during normal driving while retaining full power for acceleration when needed.
takeaways: Inactive cylinders close their valves to reduce pumping losses
Fuel consumption improvements of 5 to 15 percent are typical
Modern systems can deactivate individual cylinders dynamically

faq.question: Can drivers feel when cylinders deactivate?
faq.answer: In well-calibrated systems, the transition is nearly imperceptible. Active engine mounts and careful fueling strategies smooth the switch. Some drivers notice a subtle change in exhaust note, but vibration is minimal.

faq.question: Does cylinder deactivation cause extra engine wear?
faq.answer: When properly designed, no. Oil still circulates through deactivated cylinders. The main engineering challenge is managing the thermal variations between active and inactive cylinders to prevent uneven wear.
